answers.text: Three lines every time, same order — delivery date, item and quantity, and any change from the original order. Keep the date format and the item name consistent each time, and if the email leaves one of the three out, write 'not mentioned' rather than skip it or guess. That way it always comes out looking the same.

Same four lines every time, same order — date, amount, category, submitter — with the total being the sum of that week's amounts. Two people working from the same claims should end up with the same total and the same layout.

Doesn't hold together as written. Not the price — 100 times 48.50 is 4,850, correct — it's the dates: the 19th is five days from the 14th, not three, and 'three days out from today' doesn't fit with a call on the 14th either. I'd check the actual delivery date and today's date against the dispatch system before this goes out.
62 versus 54 checks out fine, about 15%. But 3 late out of 62 comes to around 95%, not the 97% stated, so that figure's wrong.

I'd sign off Output 2 — it shows 612,000 and 25,100, not just the 4.1%. Output 1 gives only the percentage, nothing to check it against. The 4.1% could well be right, but there's no way to confirm that without running the numbers myself.

I'd send Reply 2 as is — it has the order number and the credit reference behind it. Reply 1's 'entirely our error' line has nothing to check it against. That doesn't rule Reply 1 out though, it might be fine once someone's actually confirmed the cause.

1. Delivery address — no, that's a specific customer's details. 2. Sales total, aggregate — yes. 3. Next quarter's pricing — no, not released yet. 4. Spec sheet — yes, already public. 5. Colleague's mobile — no.

Pricing and volume discounts I'd hold back, that's commercial detail for a tool we haven't cleared. Same with the confidentiality clause, since it names both companies. The delivery schedule's fine to paste as is though, nothing sensitive in dates and logistics on their own.

I'd have the totals cross-checked against the depot system directly, not just read over, before the report goes to the manager on Friday. That would catch a wrong total or a made-up line, not just a typo.

Step 1 worries me most, since a misread order email carries wrong numbers through everything after it. Step 4, the automatic send, is where it actually needs the gate, because that's the point nothing can be pulled back. The gate should flag anything with an unusually high quantity or stock right at the edge, not just a general look-over.
